blogs.title: Push Notification Marketing: Confessions of a Strava Alum
blogs.author: Jessica Fontanilla
blogs.content: Push notification marketing: a real digital strategist's playbook Generated by Klaviyo AI Klaviyo's Jessica Fontanilla, who spent five years managing Strava's marketing tech stack before joining Klaviyo's Professional Services team, breaks down her playbook for mobile push notifications. She covers why push deserves a bigger role in the channel mix, how to grow an opted-in push audience, six message types that work for B2C brands, and how to time, sequence, and test sends across channels. Push has underused advantages: Push lands on the lock screen, carries no per-send cost once a customer has the app, and can drive real revenue — Killstar's push and email flows generated £147,027 in attributed revenue, per the case study cited. Six message types anchor the tactical playbook: Fontanilla recommends time-sensitive alerts, behavior-based nudges (viewed/cart/wishlist/search activity), welcome messages, loyalty and birthday updates, location-based geofencing, and win-back promotions for lapsed customers. Timing and sequencing follow cost and engagement: She advises starting new subscribers at one to two pushes a week, using engagement segments to message active users more often, and sequencing channels — push first, then paid channels like text or WhatsApp, then email — to protect both budget and engagement. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary Before I joined Klaviyo, I spent 5 years at Strava managing the marketing technology stack for one of the most-loved apps in fitness. At Strava, push notifications are more than a marketing tactic. They’re an actual part of the product experience. You finish a run, you get a notification. A friend gives you kudos, you get a notification. The channel feels natural because it’s built around milestone moments for the user. Then I moved into the broader B2C world at Klaviyo, and I noticed something: most brands treat mobile push notifications as an afterthought. They pour energy into email and text message marketing, launch an app, then send the occasional notification to their push audience, if they send anything at all. That's a missed opportunity, because push has advantages no other channel can match. The average ecommerce app retention rate was only 2.9–3.5% by day 30 in Q2 2026, according to AppsFlyer benchmarks . Push is one of the most direct, lowest-cost ways for brands to re-engage app customers. After nearly a decade in CRM and lifecycle marketing, here's the playbook for mobile push notifications I walk clients through: what to send, when to send it, and who should get it. 4 reasons push notifications deserves a bigger role in your channel mix Push is such an untapped channel. We tend to default to email because it's the bread and butter of so much marketing, but, in the day and age we're in, sometimes the quick snippets are more powerful. Push notifications are different from any other channel in your mix. Here are a few reasons why a mobile push strategy is worth the investment: Your push audience has already raised their hand. Someone who downloads your app and opts into notifications is telling you they want to hear from you. There's far less convincing to do with a push subscriber than with an email subscriber who may have handed over their address for a one-time discount years ago. Push lands on the lock screen. A push notification appears directly on the lock screen, along with other high-priority notifications. When your audience is looking at their phone, a push notification captures attention faster than other channels. Push doesn't add to your send costs. Text messaging and WhatsApp are strong channels, but the per-message costs can add up quickly. Once a customer has your app and opts in, reaching them via push doesn't increase your messaging spend. Push can drive significant revenue for your brand. Gothic lifestyle brand Killstar runs 50 live flows across email and push globally, with push generating £147,027 in attributed revenue . “Incorporating push messaging into Klaviyo alongside email has made our mobile engagement feel complete,” says Chloe Grant, CRM manager at Killstar. “It's helping us reach customers in moments where timing really matters, and we're already seeing the impact.” How to grow your push notification audience Nothing in this playbook matters without opted-in app users, which is where your other channels come in. Your email list, your website, and your social audience are all acquisition engines for your mobile app. Here are a few strategies I regularly recommend to get new app users: Add an app-specific email to your welcome flow. A dedicated message (“Did you know we have an app? Download it for exclusive offers”) converts new subscribers into app users at a high-interest moment. Give your audience a reason to download your app. App-exclusive drops, app-only discounts, and early access make downloading feel like joining an inner circle. Use on-site pop-ups to promote your app. Your website visitors are already engaged. A well-targeted sign-up form pointing to the app captures them without adding costs. Point organic and paid social campaigns to your app. Your social audience is already on their phone, one tap away from your app store listing. It's the shortest possible path from ad to install. 6 push notification marketing tactics that work for B2C brands With push notifications, you only get two lines of text, so you have to make each message count. These are 6 types of messages I see working well for B2C brands: 1. Time-sensitive alerts Push notifications, text messages, and WhatsApp messages are built for need-to-know, minute-by-minute communication. If a message can wait until someone checks their inbox, it can probably be an email. If it can't, it's a strong candidate for push. Think flash sales, back-in-stock alerts, and price drops. Here’s an example of a price drop push notification from apparel brand Yours Clothing , which uses bold font and emojis and personalizes the message to the recipient’s size. Source: Yours Clothing The technical advantage to these messages is deep linking. With deep links , you can route a customer from the notification to the exact product or page inside your app, not to a browser window they have to navigate through. Announce a price drop, link straight to the product, and the path to check-out gets dramatically shorter. Plus, once someone is in your app, they tend to stay and browse. 2. Nudges based on shopping behavior You can trigger a push notification for every behavioral event your app tracks, like: Viewed a product: Browsing behavior powers abandonment flows, price-drop triggers, and up-sell nudges, like, “Still thinking about the Luna boots? 👀 They're 20% off for the next 24 hours.” Added to cart but didn't buy: Cart activity drives abandoned cart pushes and can help you time an up-sell while intent is high. You can pair the push with an in-app message targeted to the same segment, like, "The Harper hoodie in your cart misses you! 🛒 Check-out takes 30 seconds." Added to a wishlist: A wishlist event is one of the strongest purchase signals available. Use it for price-drop pushes and wishlist reminder flows that say, “That item you saved is back in stock,” or “Wishlist alert: The Celeste dress dropped from $59 to $39. You saw it first!” Searched your app or site: Search activity tells you what a customer wants in their own words. If someone searched for something you don't carry yet, or misspelled something you do, a follow-up push can rescue a session that would otherwise end in frustration, like, “Looking for the Nova set? 🔍 It's back, with new colors!” Here’s an example of an abandonment push notification from fashion brand Princess Polly , which encourages the recipient to do a “double take” at the denim they were eyeing earlier. Source: Princess Polly 3. Welcome messages For customers who are new to your app, a simple welcome push (“Welcome to the app, here's what's new”) starts the relationship off on the right...

blogs.content: Klaviyo and Figma integration for brand-consistent marketing Generated by Klaviyo AI Klaviyo announced two Figma integrations at Config 2026 that connect design systems directly to marketing campaigns. A native plugin lets designers push email layouts to Klaviyo as image blocks, while the Composer AI agent can draft campaigns grounded in a brand's actual Figma components and styles—eliminating manual rebuilds and brand drift. Native plugin eliminates rebuilds: designers can push assets and email sections from Figma to Klaviyo in one step, with automatic ordering based on layer naming conventions and full provenance metadata AI drafts from your design system: Composer reads published Figma components and library styles through Figma's MCP server, grounding campaign drafts in real brand context rather than generic training data Multi-brand workflow support: agencies and enterprise teams can connect to multiple Klaviyo accounts from a single Figma file, switching between brands without re-authenticating Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary Brands invest heavily in Figma to build robust design systems to create assets, components, and email systems that represent them in the market. The moment those designs need to become marketing, the workflow often breaks. Designers export images by hand. Marketers manually slice every email into sections, download them, upload them into Klaviyo, and reassemble the design piece by piece. That ends now. At Figma Config 2026, Klaviyo announced an integration that connects a brand's Figma design system directly to Klaviyo marketing across email , text messaging , and mobile push : The Klaviyo Figma plug-in. This designer-facing plug-in pushes assets and email sections from Figma into Klaviyo as image blocks. It's free on the Figma Community and available to any Klaviyo and Figma user, globally. This integration gives brand, design, and marketing teams one path from Figma to the customer inbox, without manual rebuilds or brand drift. Push designs from Figma to Klaviyo Send assets and email sections straight from Figma into Klaviyo as image blocks, no exporting or manual uploads required. Add custom prefixes and suffixes across multiple layers at once, so every asset stays clearly tied to its campaign. And fine-tune export size, file type, and color profile right in the plugin, so what you ship matches what you designed. Send multiple assets in one go Select more than one frame, group, or component and send them all in a single job instead of exporting and uploading one asset at a time. The plug-in preserves your selection order, so the images land right next to each other in your Klaviyo image library, organized the way you built them and ready to drop into a campaign. Work across multiple brand accounts from one Figma file A single Figma user can connect to multiple Klaviyo accounts and push to any of them from the same file. Authenticate once, switch accounts in the plug-in sidebar, and keep moving. No re-authenticating per brand. No jumping to a separate browser tab to swap log-ins. That matters because large brand groups and creative agencies almost never live inside a single Klaviyo account. A parent company might run 3, 5, or 10 brand portfolios. An agency might move between 15–20 client accounts in a single week. The plugin is built for that reality: account switching happens right in the sidebar, skipping the maze of browser tabs entirely. It's a small detail that adds up fast for any team managing brands at scale. Tracey Wallace Tracey is the director of content strategy at Klaviyo. Previously, she led marketing teams for early stage start-ups from $0 to $20M in revenue, and was the former Editor-in-Chief at BigCommerce, where she helped usher in the era of omnichannel retail. She started her career in journalism at Elle.com and Mashable, reporting on the convergence of fashion and technology––or what we all call today, "ecommerce."
